groups.title: Planets
groups.explanation: These four planets are all bright enough to find with the naked eye.

groups.title: Metals known to the ancients
groups.explanation: Ancient smiths worked all of these metals long before chemistry had a name for them.

groups.title: Bright stars
groups.explanation: Each is among the brightest stars in the night sky.

sources.excerpt: Jupiter and Saturn possess nearly 90% of the non-stellar mass of the Solar System.
Earth and Mars are the only planets that orbit within the Sun's habitable zone, in which sunlight can keep surface water liquid under atmospheric pressure.
Closest to the Sun in order of increasing distance are the terrestrial planets – Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.

The metals of antiquity are the seven metals which humans had identified and found use for in prehistoric times in Africa, Europe and throughout Asia: gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, iron, and mercury.
The second brightest is Sirius at −1.46 mag.
Some stars, like Betelgeuse and Antares, are variable stars, changing their magnitude over days, months or years.
Rigel is the brightest and most massive component – and the eponym – of a star system of at least four stars that appear as a single blue-white point of light to the naked eye.
Vega has functioned as the baseline for calibrating the photometric brightness scale and was one of the stars used to define the zero point for the UBV photometric system.

editorNotes: Mercury is the crossing point, a planet and one of the metals of antiquity; the planet group is already full with Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, so Mercury goes with the metals. Lead, tin and copper are metals only, and Sirius, Vega, Rigel and Betelgeuse are stars rather than planets.
